source.title: The Ultimate AP Biology Unit 1 Review (Score a 5 on the Exam!)

segments.text: AP Biooun unit 1 is the foundation for
all of the great biology that you'll be
learning this year. In unit one, we'll
be looking at water and hydrogen
bonding, the elements of life, and the
four biomolecule families that all
living things are made of:
carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and
nucleic acids. To help you study for
this unit one test or the AP bioexam,
I've put together a checklist that you
can download at
apbiosuccess.com/checklist.
Water and hydrogen bonding. First thing
to note is that water is a polar
molecule. There's unequal electron
sharing between oxygen and hydrogen. And
so there's a partial negative region
over here. There's partial positive
regions over here. Note that hydrogen
bonds are intermolecular bonds. They're
between molecules, not within molecules
like covealent bonds or ionic bonds or
anything like that. What's happening is
that the oxygen is partially negative.
The hydrogen's partially positive and
the hydrogen bond is a weak bond that
forms between those two areas. Hydrogen
bonds are much weaker, much much weaker
than coalent bonds, ionic bonds, any of
those intramolecular
bonds. Using the diagram below as an
example, describe how hydrogen bonds can
form between molecules besides water.
The key idea is that hydrogen bonds are
everywhere. They're not just within
water. They're essential in biology in
general. So in this example, there are
two hydrogen bonds. And here's one
oxygen to hydrogen over here. Here's
another one between nitrogen and
hydrogen. This is between the
nitrogenous base adinine and thymine.
And these are the hydrogen bonds that
hold together DNA. Hydrogen bonds again
are essential. They're key to the
structure of DNA, RNA, proteins. You'll
meet them again and again throughout
your biology course, and they're
important to know for the AP bio exam as
well. So now, let's look at some of the
consequences. Describe cohesion,
adhesion, and surface tension, and
explain how these key properties of
water result from hydrogen bonding.
Cohesion. That's hydrogen bonds between
water molecules. So, this is cohesion
right here. And it's responsible for
many of water's very peculiar
properties. It's a very small molecule,
but it has a very high heat of
vaporization. Takes a lot of energy to
get water to evaporate, a high specific
heat. It can hold a lot of heat, and it
has high surface tension, which we'll
talk about below. Adhesion is water
sticking to other stuff. So like for
example here you see hydrogen bonds
between water molecule and the cellulose
walls that make up the conductive tubes
of plants which are also called xyllem.
A phenomenal thing is called
transpiration which is how water gets
pulled up to the top of trees and that's
all based on water's ability to cohhere
to other water molecules and to adhere
to the sides of the conductive tubes of
plants as water evaporates from the top.
And finally, surface tension. Here we
see a paper clip that's floating on
water. How does that work? Here's a
representation that shows that paperclip
resting on a net of water molecules that
are connected to one another by a
network of hydrogen bonds. The water
molecules and the bonds that are
connecting them are vastly enlarged. But
the point is to show how the collective
force of hydrogen bonds between the
water molecules creates the tension that
supports the paper clip. That's surface
tension. In terms of hydrogen ions,
hydroxide ions, and pH, describe the
difference between an acidic and a basic
solution. The first thing to note is
that acidic solutions are solutions that
have more hydrogen ions. Here's a
hydrogen ion over here than hydroxide
ion. That's represented by O over here.
So if you dissolve this in water, you
wind up having lots of hydrogen ions and
that pushes the pH down. The pH is below
7. In bases, there are more hydroxide
ions than hydrogen ions. So if you
dissolve sodium hydroxide in water, you
wind up with a lot more hydroxide ions
and that pushes the pH in this
direction. PH is above 7. And one thing
that I want to emphasize is that you
don't really need to know about pH for
the AP exam directly. There won't be a
question about it, but it might be part
of an FRQ or a multiple choice question.
So it's an essential underlying concept.
Elements of life, topic 1.2 of AP
biology. So what do you need to know
about the elements of life? carbon,
hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus,
and sulfur. Sometimes referred to as
chops. Carbon is the central element in
all of the molecules that make up living
things. Hydrogen often used in energy
exchange. Uh we have molecules like NAD
and NADH would show up in cellular
respiration. NAD+ is the low energy
form. NADH is the high energy form. You
see stuff like that over and over again.
And also hydrogen as an ion, as a
hydrogen ion, a proton is often pumped
around to create energy gradients. It's
very important in the synthesis of ATP.
It's the basis of acidity and alkalinity
which we just talked about. But the main
thing is to know about these atoms in
context. Phosphorus is in phosphate
groups which is found in ATP. That's the
kind of interconnected crosstopic
knowledge that you want to have for
success in AP bio. Now on to topic 1.3
monomers and polymers and functional
groups. So what are monomers? What are
polymers? The basic idea is that three
of the four groups of biomolecules
carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids
are built from smaller building blocks
that are called monomers. So here's a
glucose monomer over here. Living things

polysaccharides, and that have specific

Legos. You can combine them in any way
to create other structures. And these
big structures, the Millennium Falcon
that you might have built as a kid or
something like that, those are the
polymers. And um here's a note about
structural formulas. If you see
something like this, you might wonder

Every unspecified angle vertex has a

so central that it's just understood.
How do you put monomers together to make
polymers? It's a process that's called
dehydration synthesis. Everything in
biology is run by enzymes as we'll see
in unit three. And what enzymes do is
they pull a hydroxal group over here off
one monomer and it pulls a hydrogen off

here's the hydrogen. That water is

same thing. So two monomers becoming a

Easy to remember. Synthesis is how you
build things. And dehydration when

dehydration synthesis is pulling out a
water. Now what about hydrarolysis?
Hydraysis is the opposite of dehydration
synthesis. In biology, the suffix lice

breaking. So what happens in

isn't shown inserts a water molecule in

You add a water molecule and you get
galactose and glucose. What do you need
to know about functional groups? In one
sense, not a lot. They're not going to
directly appear on the AP bio exam, but
in another sense, they're very important
in terms of you decoding what's
happening with the molecules in biology,
which means the molecules that might
appear on the AP bio exam or in your
course. So, let's go through a couple

they're key for energy exchange. ATP,
adenosine triphosphate. Phosphates are

There are a couple of polar functional

and the amino group that's at number

Over here have a caroxile group.

macroolecules

Let's end our review of carbohydrates by

So that makes sense from an evolutionary

something that you don't eat? But what

lactase into adulthood became

questions.question: Why do most mammals produce lactase only during infancy?
questions.retryQuestion: What is the reason most mammals produce lactase only while they are infants?
questions.explanation: Most mammals drink milk only during infancy, so producing lactase later would be wasteful because the enzyme would have no substrate to act on.
choices: Because lactase production is triggered by growth hormones.
Because milk is toxic to adult mammals.
Because lactase is needed to digest solid food.
Because infancy is the only time most mammals drink milk.
questions.answer: Because infancy is the only time most mammals drink milk.

questions.question: A pleated sheet forms when parallel or antiparallel segments of a polypeptide chain interact through covalent bonds between carbonyl and amino groups.
questions.retryQuestion: A pleated sheet is stabilized by covalent bonds between carbonyl and amino groups of parallel or antiparallel polypeptide segments.
questions.explanation: The pleated sheet is stabilized by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds, between the carbonyl and amino groups of the polypeptide backbone.
questions.correction: A pleated sheet forms when parallel or antiparallel segments of a polypeptide chain interact through hydrogen bonds between carbonyl and amino groups.

questions.question: When blood becomes deoxygenated, it has given off oxygen to tissues.
questions.retryQuestion: Blood that has become deoxygenated has released its oxygen to the tissues.
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood is blood that has delivered oxygen to tissues, such as muscle during exercise.
questions.correction: When blood becomes deoxygenated, it has given off oxygen to tissues.

questions.question: Under what structural condition does lactose, a disaccharide, consist of two linked monosaccharides?
questions.retryQuestion: What is the structural composition of lactose as a disaccharide?
questions.explanation: Lactose is a disaccharide, meaning it is composed of two linked monosaccharides.
questions.answer: Lactose is a disaccharide composed of two linked monosaccharides.
rubricIdeas: Lactose is a disaccharide composed of two linked monosaccharides.

requiredIdeas: Lactose is a disaccharide composed of two linked monosaccharides.
acceptableAnswers: Lactose is a disaccharide composed of two linked monosaccharides.

questions.question: What property of a water molecule makes it polar?
questions.retryQuestion: Which statement correctly describes the polarity of a water molecule?
questions.explanation: Water is a polar molecule because it has an uneven distribution of charge, with the oxygen end being partially negative and the hydrogen ends being partially positive.
choices: It has a positive charge on oxygen and a negative charge on hydrogen.
It has no charged regions because it is a neutral molecule.
It has an uneven distribution of charge, with the oxygen end partially negative and the hydrogen ends partially positive.
It has an even distribution of charge across all atoms.
questions.answer: It has an uneven distribution of charge, with the oxygen end partially negative and the hydrogen ends partially positive.

questions.question: When phospholipids are arranged in a spherical structure in water, they form a monolayer of one phospholipid layer.
questions.retryQuestion: A spherical arrangement of phospholipids in water produces a single layer of phospholipids.
questions.explanation: The false statement changes the number of layers: the supported fact specifies a bilayer, meaning two layers, not a monolayer.
questions.correction: When phospholipids are arranged in a spherical structure in water, they form a bilayer of two phospholipid layers.

questions.question: What process is used by the acetal group to activate DNA?
questions.retryQuestion: What is the name of the process by which the acetal group activates DNA?

questions.question: How do termites and ruminants obtain glucose from cellulose?
questions.retryQuestion: What mechanism allows termites and ruminants to break down cellulose into glucose?
questions.explanation: Termites and ruminants form symbiotic relationships with microorganisms that hydrolyze the bonds in cellulose, releasing glucose monomers that can be used for energy.
questions.answer: They use symbiotic microorganisms that hydrolyze the bonds in cellulose, releasing glucose monomers.

requiredIdeas: They use symbiotic microorganisms that hydrolyze the bonds in cellulose, releasing glucose monomers.

questions.question: Mutated hemoglobin molecules form hydrophobic bonds with one another because a hydrophobic amino acid is exposed on the outside of the molecule.
questions.retryQuestion: Exposed hydrophobic amino acids on mutated hemoglobin molecules cause the molecules to form hydrophobic bonds with each other.
questions.explanation: The hydrophobic amino acid on the surface drives the molecules to associate through hydrophobic interactions, leading to fiber formation within the cells.
questions.correction: Mutated hemoglobin molecules form hydrophobic bonds with one another because a hydrophobic amino acid is exposed on the outside of the molecule.

questions.question: In molecular structure drawings, what is the convention for an unspecified angle vertex?
questions.retryQuestion: What does an unlabeled angle vertex in a structural drawing represent?
questions.explanation: In structural formulas, each angle vertex that is not explicitly labeled is understood to be a carbon atom. This convention is why a molecule like C6H12O6 can be drawn with vertices that are not marked with a C.
choices: It represents a hydrogen atom.
It represents a carbon atom.
It represents an oxygen atom.
It represents a nitrogen atom.

questions.question: Why do most mammals produce lactase only during infancy?
questions.retryQuestion: What is the reason most mammals produce lactase only while they are infants?
questions.explanation: Most mammals drink milk only during infancy, so producing lactase later would be wasteful because the enzyme would have no substrate to act on.
choices: Because lactase production is triggered by growth hormones.
Because milk is toxic to adult mammals.
Because lactase is needed to digest solid food.
Because infancy is the only time most mammals drink milk.
questions.answer: Because infancy is the only time most mammals drink milk.

questions.question: A pleated sheet forms when parallel or antiparallel segments of a polypeptide chain interact through covalent bonds between carbonyl and amino groups.

questions.correction: A pleated sheet forms when parallel or antiparallel segments of a polypeptide chain interact through hydrogen bonds between carbonyl and amino groups.

questions.retryQuestion: Which statement correctly describes the polarity of a water molecule?

It has no charged regions because it is a neutral molecule.
It has an uneven distribution of charge, with the oxygen end partially negative and the hydrogen ends partially positive.
It has an even distribution of charge across all atoms.
questions.answer: It has an uneven distribution of charge, with the oxygen end partially negative and the hydrogen ends partially positive.
